Happy Fathers' Day! Is it just father's day? - I never bothered to look it up, but I've always thought of it as plural. I honor my dad and expect my kids to honor him... and if my grandfathers were alive, I'd honor them and expect my kids to do so as well.

Got me thinking about how it's totally a Hallmark holiday created to sell cards, but is something we should actually embrace. It's dad who made you who you are and as dad you'll make your kids into who they'll grow to be.

With all the news recently about "pride month" and this race-to-the-bottom, I started thinking more about "culture" and how we arrived at the current social-temporal point. It's kinda our fault. Maybe not yours and mine, but that of our generations... The late boomers and early gen-Xers completely failed their kids... and those are the young-adults shaping our world today. The historical culture was replaced by pop-culture and that's probably what is responsible for the decline... but I digress.

The reason I brought up culture is that I was thinking about my dad and the early lessons in life... The regional cultural things which define a man where I live... and that got me thinking about what else contributes to that "culture" - the history, the work-ethic, the food, the art, the music. It was really the music that hit me. I think that's a cultural piece which really defines everyone. I realized that I judge people based on their musical tastes... but it's not the actual music. It's my perception of the ideology behind the music as well as the actual artistic properties.

I started kind of drifting back to the songs I'd hear in my dad's '79 cadillac as a kid and it was all bluesy, rock-and-roll with a twang or even proper outlaw-country. and like any kid I rebelled against it and decided I liked hip-hop and punk-rock and anything "Edgy" long before we called it by such a name. I wanted to be the opposite of everything my dad wanted me to be and I think that's fairly common. I started to come back around in my mid-20s but didn't really see the value in anything my father tried to teach me until I became a dad myself.

Over the past decade-ish of fatherhood I've really grown to appreciate the lessons my dad shared. Learning to slaughter a hog and butcher it properly, how to smoke and cure various meats, how to fix appliances, engines and early electronics... how to shake hands, how to look a man in the eye, how to introduce yourself to a room... how to bait a hook and hold a shotgun close-in on your shoulder so you don't blow it out of socket the first time you shoot (he handed 100lb, 10-year-old me a 12 gauge and laughed with my uncles when I took a full jump-step back to avoid falling-over from the kick)

But looking back, it was the music. It's the sound that defined the culture... I kept an i-pod full of 90s-2000s punk-rock and hip-hop in my truck for like 15 years... and over the past 7-8 years I was listening less and less frequently. I spent more time in the truck tuned into the classic-rock station. Today I find that when I want to listen to music I gravitate towards the 70s-rock or southern rock sound and it's the sound I want my kids to grow-up hearing. I hooked up an old receiver in the garage and wired it to the old in-house speaker system which was rigged to this place when we moved in (it's cutting-edge 1995-ish technology).

Anyway I think it's sort of a "songs of my people" kind of thing... and if you expose your kids to music and attitude from that time in history when we defined culture maybe they'll feel enough pride in it to defend it against this seemingly unending onslaught... and you'll be proud when your grandkids and great grandkids call or visit to say "happy fathers day"
